rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 report the authors' own field experiments on four sod fields in North Carolina (randomized complete block, four replications) comparing UAV weed mapping plus UAV site-specific spraying with ground broadcast spraying.
rows.notes: The study never measures crop productivity, yield or any sustainability outcome; trials were on out-of-production or weed-free sod with potted tobacco as surrogate weeds. What it shows is that UAV-derived weed maps allow a UAV sprayer to treat 20-60% less area than broadcast while missing up to 26% of target weeds (Tables 1-2), i.e. an input-saving precondition, not a crop-production effect. Monitoring was done once pre-application and at 14 and 28 DAT, but scalability/rapidity/repeatability of surveillance are not evaluated as outcomes.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, own field experiments with UAV-IS vs ground broadcast glufosinate applications. Q2: Abstract and Tables 1-2: UAV weed maps (supervised classification, Fig 1-2) used to build prescription flight paths; UAV-IS sprayed 77% vs 98% of plot area (natural weeds) and 33% vs 93% (surrogate weeds), treating only 30% of non-weedy area vs 92% for broadcast, i.e. less herbicide and less off-target treatment; Section 3.2 states the UAV-IS treated 60% less area. Q4: Section 2.4 and Tables 1-2 quantify the intermediate variables - area sprayed, precision, recall, false positives/negatives from overlaying weed maps and injury maps - and Section 3.2 links the saving to weed spatial aggregation. Q7: Section 3.2 and 3.4/Conclusion state that application efficiency rises with weed patch aggregation and that pesticide reduction applies where weed distribution is clearly aggregated and broadcast is not justified; efficacy depends on weed distribution and morphology. Q8: Section 3.3 reports up to 1 m deviation from target due to UAV GPS accuracy (no RTK), up to 26% of weedy area missed; Section 2.2 acknowledges arbitrary targeting criteria (patches >1 m, >35% cover, max three passes); Conclusion notes the system requires several software and technical processes; Section 3.4 notes payload and battery limits.
rows.notes: Mechanical control and operational costs are not evaluated; support is for precision herbicide application and reduced treated/off-target area only. Q3 no: sprayed-area results derive from one image-overlay method (ground checks only verified the injury map); tobacco dry weights concern efficacy, not input reduction. Q5 no: two NC locations with results reported for two studies, not three or more sites. Q6 no: 100-136 m2 plots. Q9 no: tables give means and p-values only, no SD/CI.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a plot-scale field evaluation of an integrated UAV mapping-plus-UAV spraying system in turf sod; efficacy was lower for UAV-IS on natural weeds (81% vs 97% injury) but higher on surrogate tobacco, so chemical reduction came with a recall trade-off.
